english.html: not only those who give, sell or buy a free person <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, but also those who conceal, imprison or detain one, or otherwise abuse her <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>: a crime beyond doubt capital, deserving death by the law of God. WHOEVER SHALL HAVE stolen (says the Lord) any of his brethren, and afterwards sold him, or otherwise abused him, he shall die the death <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>; which singularly has place when such a theft has been made of a person near to, and closely joined with, another by some great bond of nature, as a child or a wife <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. And it is nothing to say that the said de Rols was detained of her own will, seeing that she never gainsaid it <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>, but rather always vigorously maintained that it was her husband. For, by what has been said a little before, that is not, properly speaking, will, since it is forced and extorted by ruses, cunning and seductions <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 48.15 (Ad legem Fabiam de plagiariis; Coras's Fau., Favia), ll. 1, 3 and the penultimate law; Code 9.20 (Ad legem Fabiam de plagiariis), l. Quoniam servos (fragment number unverified) and the penultimate law of the same title
notes.original: l. j. l. iij. l. pen. D ad l. Fau. de plagia. l. quoniã ſeruos. l. pe. c. au meſme ti tre.
notes.gloss: The lex Fabia punishes the selling, buying, giving or hiding of a free man or of another's slave.

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 1 (D. 43.29.1, Ulpian); and the places already cited (Annotation 83, notes g and following)
notes.original: l. j. D. de libe. ho. exhi. & aux autres lieux. ia alleguez.
notes.gloss: The praetor's interdict: quem liberum dolo malo retines, exhibeas — produce the free man you wrongfully detain.
Whoever steals one of his brethren of the children of Israel and sells him shall die.

notes.citation: Code 9.20 (Ad legem Fabiam de plagiariis), the last law (C. 9.20.16, Constantine)
notes.gloss: Plagiarii, qui viventium filiorum miserandas infligunt parentibus orbitates — the kidnappers who inflict on parents the pitiable loss of living children are condemned, if slaves or freedmen, to the beasts, if free, to the sword; whence Coras's "as a child or a wife".

notes.citation: Digest 24.3 (Soluto matrimonio dos quemadmodum petatur), l. 2, § Voluntatem (D. 24.3.2.2, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ij. P. volũ tatem. D. ſol. mat.
notes.gloss: Whether the daughter's "will", when her father sues for the dowry, means that she consents or only that she does not object: by a rescript of Antoninus she is taken to consent unless she evidently contradicts — nisi evidenter contradicat, videri consentire.

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 3, § Si quis volentem (cf. D. 43.29.3.5, Ulpian; paragraph number unverified), as at Annotation 83 {g}
notes.original: l. iij. P. ſi ꝗs volentem. D. de lib. ho. exhib.
notes.gloss: The ꝗ is the q with a stroke, the sign for qui-: si quis.

english.html: As for the pillage and theft, it is evident in this case, not only of the property, part of which this venerable impostor devoured and sold to one and another, but also of the honour of the said Martin and de Rols. I shall be told that theft is not a capital crime, still less worthy of death. Which, by the usage of the Lacedaemonians and Egyptians (who leave all thefts unpunished), would be indubitable <sup class="mk" data-key="a2">a2</sup>; nay, even according to our laws, I confess it: for Justinian himself has protested that he does not wish anyone to die for theft, nor to have any limb cut off, but that he be otherwise punished at the discretion of the Judge <sup class="mk" data-key="b2">b2</sup>. Nevertheless this is to be understood of simple thefts, which no legislator whatsoever (Draco alone excepted) has found worthy of death, but only punishable in money, at double, triple, fourfold or fivefold <sup class="mk" data-key="c2">c2</sup>, or else by some light correction <sup class="mk" data-key="d2">d2</sup>; because they reckoned (as I believe) that thefts, or the most part of them, were committed more through want and necessity than with

notes.citation: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18; Pietro Crinito (Petrus Crinitus), De honesta disciplina, book 3, c. 13 (or c. 12 — the two readings of the print; not checked)
notes.original: Aule Gelle liu. xj. c. xviij. Pierre Crinit liure iij. c. xiij.
notes.gloss: Gellius 11.18 is the chapter on the law of theft: Draco's capital penalty, Solon's double, the Egyptians who allowed every theft and the Lacedaemonians who trained their young in it.

notes.citation: Novel 134 (Ut nulli iudicum liceat habere loci servatores), the last chapter (Nov. 134.13), in the Authenticum, coll. 9; the authentica Sed novo iure in Code 6.1 (De servis fugitivis)
notes.original: P fi. vt nul li iu. aux nou uelles coll. ix. Aut. ſed nouo iure. C. de ſer. fug.
notes.gloss: Justinian forbids the mutilation of thieves: no one is to lose a limb for theft, but to be otherwise chastised. The authentica carries the rule into the Code's title on fugitive slaves. The print's iu. abbreviates iudicum, the Novel's incipit.

notes.citation: Exodus 22 (22:1–4: the restitution of double, fourfold and fivefold); Institutes 4.6 (De actionibus), § Quadrupli (cf. Inst. 4.6.21; paragraph number unverified)
notes.original: Exode c. xxij. P. quadrupli. de act.
notes.gloss: The actions for theft lie for double or fourfold the value.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2 (De furtis), l. Servi et filii (cf. D. 47.2.17, Ulpian; number unverified); Digest 48.19 (De poenis), l. In servorum (D. 48.19.10, Macer) and l. Capitalium, § Non omnes (D. 48.19.28, Callistratus; the paragraph not identified); Gellius, Attic Nights, book 11, c. 18, as at {a2}
notes.original: l. ſerui & fi lij. D. de fur. l in ſeruorum. l. capitalium. P. nõ omnes D. de pœn. Gelle au liure xi. c. xviij.
notes.gloss: The De poenis texts fix the lighter, non-capital punishments of slaves and of the humble.
